Thank you, Keith.

I'm a little bit lost with the interpretation of this syntax in
modification indexes.

1) As you can see in my original question, the highest modification
index is huge:

visimpw1 ~1 142942.937

First of all: Can I trust such a big MI? Wouldn't it be meaning that
something is radically wrong with the model, although it is identified
and converged?
If I can, should I introduce visimpw1 ~1 in the model? This is the
message I get when I do that: 'The information matrix could not be
inverted.'

2) hosp3y ~*~ hosp3y has a very large MI in my model.

I read in the model.syntax help file: 'Scale factors are used in the
Delta parameterization, in a multiple group analysis when factor
indicators are categorical.'. I'm not carrying out multiple group
analysis, although my indicators are categorical. Should I discard
this MI?

Ángel

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of operators of modification indexes
parts:
Angel,
Discussion of your model spans multiple subject headings across two email lists (of which I am aware).  It is more than I can keep up with.  I would suggest that you follow the strategy of starting with a simple model that works and building up piece by piece, as I suggested on SEMNET.  As I said there, it is easier to debug and re-specify elements of a model in isolation.  You have a very large model with many moving parts.  Remember Jim Steiger's (2002) warning about constraints interacting in unanticipated ways in complex models (Psychological Methods).

I am a little puzzled why you continue using the <~ syntax after others have warned against its use.  That is just one more wild-card in the mix.  I would use the alternative syntax provided earlier in the discussion. Relatedly, my general advice is to carefully examine the parameter table (use lavaanify() directly) and parameter matrices (use lavInspect(object, what='free')) as a way to check that you and lavaan are parsing your model syntax the same way.  This can help minimize surprises when you inspect the results of fitting the model.

Keith

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of operators of modification indexes
parts:
Modification indices are not intelligent quantities. They try to
add/free parameters (even if this makes the model non-identified) just
to see what would happen (approximately) to the chi-square test statistic.

In other words, you can safely ignore nonsensical modification indices.
In your setting, visimpw1~1 does not make sense. Just ignore it. And
because you are in the single-group setting, you don't need scaling
parameters, so you can also ignore hosp3y ~*~ hosp3y.

Yves.
